analysis.one_liner: Requires your explicit permission before credit bureaus can share your credit report with anyone.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote in the Senate Banking Committee and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Today, credit reporting companies can sell your credit report to lenders, insurers, and marketers unless you tell them to stop. This bill would flip that: nobody could pull your report for a credit or insurance decision, or for unsolicited offers, unless you first gave informed permission and the company verified who you were. It would also ban credit bureaus from charging consumers fees for report-related services and require them to take real steps to prevent data breaches.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers whose credit files are bought and sold without their say-so. Under the bill, your credit report could only be released for a new loan, insurance underwriting, or an unsolicited credit offer if you affirmatively consented and your identity was verified [S2][S3]. You could revoke consent, the process had to be free and accessible by phone or secure electronic means, and bureaus could not charge you any fee for these activities [S3]. Bureaus would also have to use commercially reasonable efforts to prevent unauthorized access to your file, and a GAO study would identify further protections needed [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers whose credit files are sold

how_it_helps.text: Reverses the default: instead of consumers having to opt out of having their reports shared, credit bureaus would need affirmative, verified consent before sharing a report for credit, insurance underwriting, or unsolicited firm offers [S2][S3].

Bans fees: consumer reporting agencies could not charge consumers any fee for activities under the bill, including providing or revoking consent, and bureaus had to offer a secure, cost-free method (toll-free phone or secure electronic means) that takes effect within one business day [S3].

Tightens data security: bureaus must use commercially reasonable efforts to avoid unauthorized access to consumer reports, following Gramm-Leach-Bliley standards, and the GAO must study what further protections are needed for information in consumer files [S2][S3].

Cuts unsolicited 'prescreened' credit and insurance offers: a record of inquiries from transactions you did not initiate generally could not be furnished, and your name and address could only appear on marketing lists you elected into [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Credit reporting agencies like Experian, Equifax, and TransUnion, which would lose the default right to sell consumer reports and marketing lists and would have to build consent-verification systems. Lenders, insurers, and marketers that rely on prescreened lists to find customers would lose that pipeline, and instant credit approvals could get slower when consent must be gathered first [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: Opt-in consent could slow credit: much of today's lending (pre-approval at a checkout counter, instant insurance quotes) depends on pulling reports without delay; requiring verified consent beforehand could add friction to loans and offers some consumers actually want [S3].
Compliance costs: bureaus and lenders would have to build consent systems, identity verification, and one-business-day processing, and some of that cost could show up in the price of credit [S3].

The security mandate is soft: the bill requires 'commercially reasonable efforts' to prevent breaches rather than a hard, enforceable standard, and much of the bill's consumer-protection work is delegated to future CFPB rulemaking [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers, the upside is real control over who sees their credit file, no fees, and stronger breach protection, at the cost of some friction in getting credit and losing some prescreened offers. The burden falls on a small, concentrated industry that has profited from the current opt-out default, so the trade-off favors ordinary people; the main weakness is that enforcement depends on later regulation and a soft security standard.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Banking Committee, which never considered it, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Jack Reed introduced the Consumer Credit Control Act of 2023 on April 26, 2023, with Senator Chris Van Hollen as cosponsor [S1][S4].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs; no further action was ever taken on the bill [S5].
The committee never held a markup or a vote, and the bill never reached the Senate floor before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit bureaus and the lenders, insurers, and marketers that buy prescreened consumer data. Because the bill died, the current opt-out system stays in place and their access to consumer credit files is unchanged.

for.name: Sen. Jack Reed
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its sole sponsor.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Sen. Sherrod Brown, D-OH)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; it sat there until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill had only two Democratic sponsors and no Republican or additional support, so no partisan split appears in the record.

industries.note: Bureaus would lose the default right to sell consumer reports for credit, insurance, and prescreened marketing lists, and would have to build free consent and identity-verification systems. Their data-sale business model depends on the opt-out status quo this bill would have ended [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Lenders, insurers, and marketers using prescreened lists
industries.note: They would lose unsolicited access to consumer files for marketing firm offers, cutting off a major customer-acquisition channel; some consumers would also see fewer pre-approved offers. Legitimate lending would still be possible but only after obtaining consent [S3].
